specs.label: Frame generation
specs.help: Draws new frames between the ones the game sends, so a 30 fps game moves like 60, 90 or 120 fps. Off shows the stream exactly as it arrives. In the video window, I turns it off and on for this session only, to compare.

impact.picture: Smoother motion. Small, fast details can wobble a little.
impact.speed: Adds delay: about 20 ms at 60 fps, about 40 ms at 90 or 120 fps.

choices.name: Off
choices.hint: No new frames: the stream exactly as the game sends it, with the least delay.

specs.label: Output frame rate
specs.help: How many frames you see each second. Higher is smoother, but needs a faster graphics card and a display that runs at least that fast (G-Sync or FreeSync helps). Auto-detect, on SmoovPlay's Settings page, picks the most this PC keeps up with.

choices.name: 60 fps
choices.hint: One new frame for each real one. Any supported graphics card, any display. Adds about 20 ms of delay.

choices.name: 90 fps
choices.hint: Two new frames for each real one. Needs a 90 Hz or faster display. Adds about 40 ms of delay.

choices.name: 120 fps
choices.hint: Three for each real one. Needs a 120 Hz display and a fast card. Adds about 40 ms of delay.

specs.label: Even out 40-60 fps
specs.help: For games that run between about 40 and 60 fps, like unlocked performance modes. Their frames arrive unevenly, some staying on screen twice as long as others, so motion stutters. SmoovPlay times each one and draws evenly spaced frames from them at 60, 90 or 120 fps. 30 fps and 60 fps games aren't affected. Experimental: not tried with a real game yet.

impact.picture: Even motion in 40-60 fps games, instead of stutter.
impact.speed: About one frame (17 ms) more delay than showing their frames as they come.

specs.label: Game frame rate
specs.help: Auto works out the game's frame rate from the stream as it plays. A still or dark scene can fool it into reading a 30 fps game as 40 or more, which makes motion uneven. If you know the game is locked at 30 fps (most console quality modes), pick 30 fps: every other frame is taken as new, so motion stays even. Menus that run at 60 fps look a little less smooth with it.

impact.picture: Even motion in a game locked at 30 fps, whatever the scene.
impact.speed: None. At most one frame (17 ms) later for a moment after the game stutters.

choices.name: Auto
choices.hint: SmoovPlay works out the game's frame rate as it plays. The default.

choices.name: 30 fps
choices.hint: For a game locked at 30 fps. Every other frame is taken as new, so nothing can misread it.

specs.label: Dip smoothing
specs.help: For 30 fps games that sometimes drop below 30, as some big open-world games do on a base console. At each dip a frame stays up longer and the next one jumps. With this on, SmoovPlay spaces the frames it draws by when the game's frames arrived, so a dip looks like a brief slow-down instead. It's only on while the game dips, and adds delay then.

impact.picture: A dip below 30 fps looks like a brief slow-down, not a freeze and a jump.
impact.speed: While it dips: 17 to 50 ms more delay, and more graphics card work.

specs.label: Interpolation model
specs.help: The AI model that draws the in-between frames. RIFE 4.22 lite is the one SmoovPlay is tuned and tested with, fast enough for 90 and 120 fps. NVIDIA VFG (Video Frame Generation) is NVIDIA's own, for RTX 40 and 50 series cards: SmoovPlay's Settings page downloads it from NVIDIA once you accept NVIDIA's licence.
specs.later: Support for other interpolation models may come in a later version.

choices.name: RIFE 4.22 lite
choices.hint: Fast and tested. The default.

choices.name: NVIDIA VFG
choices.hint: NVIDIA's own frame generation, for RTX 40 and 50 series cards. A separate download from NVIDIA.

specs.label: VFG quality
specs.help: How much work NVIDIA VFG puts into each in-between frame. Higher takes more of your graphics card's time, which can cost in-between frames at 90 and 120 fps. Only used with NVIDIA VFG.

choices.name: Low
choices.hint: The lightest on your graphics card.

choices.name: Medium
choices.hint: Balanced. The default.

choices.name: High
choices.hint: The most careful, and the heaviest.

specs.label: Steady HUD
specs.help: Keeps the parts of the picture that don't move, like the map, health bar and subtitles, exactly as the game drew them, so they don't wobble when the scene behind them moves. Results vary by game, and often there's no visible difference. If a small, fast object ever flickers, turn it off.

impact.picture: Steadier HUD in some games; in others, slightly worse elsewhere.
impact.speed: About 0.5 ms more work per real frame, and a little more delay.

specs.label: AI engine
specs.help: The software that runs the AI model on your graphics card. Both draw the same frames; only the speed differs. Auto uses TensorRT at full motion detail, where it's about 12% faster, and PyTorch at half, where PyTorch is faster. Only used with RIFE.

impact.picture: None: both draw the same frames.
impact.speed: TensorRT is about 12% faster at full motion detail, PyTorch at half.

choices.name: Auto
choices.hint: The faster one for your settings. Recommended.

choices.name: TensorRT
choices.hint: Fastest at full motion detail. Its first start on a graphics card takes a minute or two.

choices.name: PyTorch
choices.hint: Starts at once. Fastest at half motion detail.

specs.label: Motion detail
specs.help: How finely RIFE tracks movement. Full follows small, fast details best, like railings or distant cars; Half takes about 40% less time but softens them a little. Auto uses Half at 120 fps, for a 1440p capture at 90, or where Auto-detect timed Full too slow for your graphics card at the frame rate you picked; a quarter for a 4K capture; and Full otherwise. Only used with RIFE.

impact.picture: Half is a little softer on small, fast details.
impact.speed: Half takes about 40% less time per AI frame.

choices.name: Auto
choices.hint: Full; Half at 120 fps, a 1440p capture at 90, or where Full is too slow for this card; less for 4K. Recommended.

choices.name: Full
choices.hint: Sharpest on fast motion. The slowest.

choices.name: Half
choices.hint: About 40% faster. A little softer on fast detail.

specs.label: Simulate a 30 fps game
specs.help: For testing with a 60 fps game: every other frame is left out, so it plays like a 30 fps game. At 60 and 120 fps each AI frame is also scored against the real frame it replaced. For a game locked at 30 fps, use Game frame rate: 30 fps instead. This session only.

specs.label: Upscaler
specs.help: Enlarges the picture from the game (usually 1080p) to fill your window or screen, so it only matters when that's bigger than 1080p, like a 1440p or 4K display. Key: U.
specs.later: Support for other upscalers may come in a later version.

impact.picture: Only matters on a display bigger than the stream, like 1440p or 4K.
impact.speed: About 0.1 ms a frame for FSR 1. RTX VSR runs an AI model on every frame, which can cost in-between frames at 90 and 120 fps.

choices.name: AMD FSR 1
choices.hint: Sharp and almost free: about 0.1 ms a frame. Recommended.

choices.name: NVIDIA RTX VSR
choices.hint: NVIDIA's AI upscaler, Experimental. It comes with NVIDIA VFG's download (RTX 40 and 50 series); without it, FSR 1 is used. Heavier.

choices.name: Bilinear
choices.hint: Plain resizing, the softest. For comparison.

specs.label: FSR sharpening
specs.help: How strongly FSR 1 sharpens the enlarged picture. More looks crisper; less keeps the blocky patches of a weak Wi-Fi stream from standing out. Only used with AMD FSR 1.

impact.picture: More is crisper; less keeps a blocky stream calmer.
impact.speed: No difference.

choices.name: Max
choices.hint: Crispest. Can make compression blocks stand out.

choices.name: Medium
choices.hint: Balanced. The default.

choices.name: Minimal
choices.hint: Softest. Best for a blocky, low-quality stream.

specs.label: RTX VSR quality
specs.help: How hard RTX VSR works to clean up and sharpen the picture. Higher looks cleaner but asks more of the GPU, which can cost in-between frames at 90 and 120 fps. Only used with RTX VSR, which comes with NVIDIA VFG's download from NVIDIA. On a capture card's uncompressed picture it uses NVIDIA's models for clean video.

impact.speed: Each step up asks more of the GPU.

specs.label: HDR
specs.help: Experimental: not yet tried with a real PS5 HDR stream, or on an HDR screen. For Remote Play in HDR, pick the H.265 HDR codec in chiaki-ng, then turn this on. Shown in SDR fits HDR to any display. HDR output keeps it HDR on a display with Use HDR on in Windows (without one, it's shown in SDR). A stream without HDR isn't changed. Applies the next time you press Play.

impact.picture: An HDR stream's true colours, instead of a washed-out picture.
impact.speed: About 0.7 ms of graphics card time for each frame from the game.

choices.name: Off
choices.hint: For a stream without HDR. The default.

choices.name: On, shown in SDR
choices.hint: Plays an HDR stream on any display, with its colours and brightness fitted to it.

choices.name: On, HDR output
choices.hint: Keeps it HDR on an HDR display, with Use HDR on in Windows' display settings. Not yet tried on an HDR screen.

specs.label: Capture card resolution
specs.help: Capture cards only (Remote Play is 1080p at most). Higher is sharper on a bigger screen, but every new frame is drawn at this size, so it can run quite sluggish. A capture bigger than your screen gains nothing. The console must send it too. Experimental; applies the next time you press Play.

impact.picture: Sharper on a 1440p or 4K screen; no gain on a 1080p one.
impact.speed: 1440p: about twice the work of 1080p. 4K: about four times. Both can run sluggish.

elsewhere.chiaki: Only used with a capture card. PS5 Remote Play streams 1080p at most.
elsewhere.window: Only used with a capture card. App window capture is scaled to 1080p.
elsewhere.tap: Only used with a capture card. The app sends its frames at its own size.
elsewhere: Only used with a capture card.

choices.name: 1080p
choices.hint: The lightest: 60, 90 or 120 fps on a fast card. Recommended. The default.

choices.name: 1440p
choices.hint: About twice the work of 1080p: fine at 60 fps on most cards, but 90 can run sluggish. Sharper on a 1440p or 4K screen.

choices.name: 4K
choices.hint: About four times the work of 1080p: likely to run sluggish, even at 60 fps on a fast card. Only for a 4K screen.

specs.label: Look
specs.help: Effects on top of the picture, like a color grade, film grain or bloom: one of SmoovPlay's looks, or your own, made on SmoovPlay's Looks page. K turns the look on and off, J goes to the next one. Saved clips stay as the game looked unless Looks in clips is on.

impact.picture: Changes the colors and style of the picture, the way you choose.
impact.speed: About 0.02 to 0.35 ms a frame of graphics card time for SmoovPlay's looks (1440p).

specs.label: Which look
specs.help: The look to use: SmoovPlay's own, then the ones you made or pasted on the Looks page. J goes to the next one, Shift+J back.

specs.label: Fullscreen
specs.help: Fills the whole screen. It also skips the Windows desktop compositor, which removes about 12 ms of delay, so it's the best way to play. Key: F.

impact.speed: About 12 ms less delay than a window, and G-Sync or FreeSync works.

specs.label: Fill the screen
specs.help: For an ultrawide screen. Consoles send 16:9 only, so none of these is real ultrawide: there's no more of the game to show. They crop or stretch the same 16:9 picture. Key: Z.

impact.picture: The same 16:9 picture, cropped or stretched: consoles send 16:9 only.
impact.speed: No real difference. Panorama adds one pass over the screen: about 0.02 ms.

choices.name: Fit
choices.hint: All of the picture, true to shape, with black bars on an ultrawide. The default.

choices.name: Zoom
choices.hint: Fills the screen by cutting off the top and bottom of the picture, which can cut the HUD.

choices.name: Stretch
choices.hint: Fills the screen by making everything wider.

choices.name: Panorama
choices.hint: The middle stays close to true shape and the sides take the stretch, like a TV's wide zoom. Ultrawide only.

specs.label: VSync
specs.help: Off: the lowest delay, but fast camera turns can show a tear line across the picture. On: no tearing, with a little more delay. With a G-Sync or FreeSync display, On gives you both: no tearing and low delay.

impact.speed: On can add up to one refresh of delay: 8 ms at 120 Hz, 17 at 60.

specs.label: Window presentation
specs.help: How the video reaches the screen. In a window, Standard goes through the Windows compositor, which adds about 12 ms and keeps G-Sync and FreeSync from working. Low delay hands frames over the way games do, for playing in a window; fullscreen uses Standard, as quick there. With Windows' HDR on, it's always Low delay, so fullscreen keeps HDR on. Experimental; applies the next time you press Play.

impact.speed: Low delay should save the 12 ms a window adds. Still being measured.

choices.name: Standard
choices.hint: OpenGL's own way. Tested. In a window, Windows adds a copy of each frame.

choices.name: Low delay (Experimental)
choices.hint: Hands frames over the way games do, so a window is about as quick as fullscreen and G-Sync works. Experimental.

specs.label: Stats overlay
specs.help: Numbers in a corner of the video: how many frames a second are on screen, the game's own frame rate, and whether your PC keeps up. Key: S (Off, Minimal, Detailed).

specs.label: Stats overlay style
specs.help: Minimal: frames on screen, the game's frame rate (amber when it isn't 30 fps) and the delay, with a dot: green, your PC keeps up; amber, it's tight; red, it's falling behind, so try a lower frame rate. Detailed adds the AI frame time, the upscaler and, at 90 and 120 fps, the extra frames shown (below about 95%, your PC is falling behind).

choices.name: Minimal
choices.hint: A small line: frames on screen, the game's frame rate, the delay, and a dot for how well your PC keeps up.

choices.name: Detailed
choices.hint: Everything: AI frame time, the upscaler, and at 90 and 120 fps the share of extra frames shown.

specs.label: Stats overlay position
specs.help: The corner the stats go in, tucked into its edges. Pick one your game's own HUD leaves free.

specs.label: Stats overlay size
specs.help: How big the stats are. Small stays out of the way of the game's own HUD; Large is for a TV across the room.

choices.name: Small
choices.hint: Out of the way of the game's own HUD.

choices.name: Medium
choices.hint: Easier to read from further away.

choices.name: Large
choices.hint: For a TV across the room.

specs.label: Instant replay
specs.help: Keeps the last stretch of what you played, so you can save it after something good happens: press R in the video window, or Ctrl+Alt+R from anywhere. Clips go to your Videos folder, in SmoovPlay, as MP4 at the frame rate you see, with the game's own sound (PS5 Remote Play and capture cards; window capture has none). B saves a before & after video instead.

impact.speed: About 0.3 ms of graphics card time a frame; the encoding is on its video encoder, not the AI's part.

choices.name: Off
choices.hint: Nothing is kept.

choices.name: Last 30 seconds
choices.hint: Keeps about 160 MB in memory (1080p at 90 fps).

choices.name: Last minute
choices.hint: Keeps about 310 MB in memory (1080p at 90 fps).

choices.name: Last 2 minutes
choices.hint: Keeps about 610 MB in memory (1080p at 90 fps).

choices.name: Last 5 minutes
choices.hint: Keeps about 1.5 GB in memory (1080p at 90 fps).

specs.label: Saved clip
specs.help: What R saves. SmoovPlay video is what you saw, at 60, 90 or 120 fps. Before & after puts the game's own frames next to SmoovPlay's in one video, to show the difference; it's made in the background and takes about as long as the clip. B always saves a before & after video.

choices.name: SmoovPlay video
choices.hint: What you saw, with the game's sound. Saved in a second or two.

choices.name: Before & after
choices.hint: The game's own frames next to SmoovPlay's, in one video. Made in the background, in about as long as the clip.

choices.name: Both
choices.hint: Both videos.

specs.label: Before & after layout
specs.help: How a before & after video is laid out. Split screen is one picture: the left half as the game sent it, the right half from SmoovPlay, with a line between. Side by side shows both whole pictures, in a video twice as wide.

choices.name: Split screen
choices.hint: One picture: the left half as the game sent it, the right half from SmoovPlay.

choices.name: Side by side
choices.hint: Both whole pictures next to each other, in a video twice as wide.

specs.label: Looks in clips
specs.help: Puts the look you're using into saved clips too. Off keeps clips as the game looked, whatever look you play with. In a before & after video, only the SmoovPlay side gets the look.

impact.picture: Clips look like what you see, look included.
impact.speed: Up to about 0.2 ms more a frame of graphics card time, to draw it again at 1080p.

specs.label: Minimise chiaki-ng
specs.help: Minimises chiaki-ng's own window while SmoovPlay's video is open, so your graphics card doesn't spend time drawing a copy nobody sees. chiaki-ng keeps streaming, playing sound and reading your controller, and its window comes back when you stop.

impact.speed: Saves the time your graphics card spends drawing chiaki-ng's window.

elsewhere: Only used with PS5 Remote Play.

specs.label: Sound in sync
specs.help: The sound (chiaki-ng's, or a capture card's, which SmoovPlay plays) would come as it arrives, while the picture spends a little longer in SmoovPlay. On holds the sound back by that time (about 30 ms at 90 fps, measured as you play), so they line up. Press L in the video window for a delay test: it times the whole trip, from a button press to SmoovPlay's screen (PS5 Remote Play).

impact.speed: None: only the sound waits, by as long as the picture does.
